abstract: Soil-transmitted helminths infect over 1 billion people worldwide, yet how dormant infective larvae sense entry into a host and exit developmental arrest to establish infection remains largely unknown. Here, in the human parasite Strongyloides stercoralis, we identify L-cystine as a host signal that stimulates larval feeding and synthesis of dafachronic acid, a steroid hormone that activates DAF-12 and promotes post-infection development. A CRISPR screen of candidate receptors identified a previously uncharacterized olfactory GPCR, Ss-OR1, that is activated by L-cystine in heterologous cells and required for a normal L-cystine-induced feeding response in the parasite. Surprisingly, L-cystine also activated an OR1 homolog from the insect parasite Steinernema carpocapsae and stimulated feeding in its infective larvae. These findings identify L-cystine as a conserved host signal that activates OR1 homologs and stimulates feeding in nematodes infecting evolutionarily distant hosts.
